rana.notes: Your mother. Teaches Arabic at a school in Nablus.

bassam.notes: Your father. Drives to work through a checkpoint he cannot predict.

nawal.notes: Your grandmother. Bakes on a taboun her mother built.

abeer.notes: Your teacher. Marks forty exercise books by torchlight when the power goes.

samir.notes: Your friend since the waste ground. Wants to be a physiotherapist.

huda.notes: Registered in Gaza. Married you in Ramallah, where she is not allowed to live.

khalil.notes: Sells permits that are supposed to be free. Takes a third of the wage.

clerk.notes: Interior ministry counter. Types what she hears.

soldier.notes: Nineteen. Cold. Holds the turnstile switch.

dco.notes: Behind the glass at the coordination office. Answers in one word.

farouk.notes: Oncologist in East Jerusalem. Writes the referral and knows the odds on the permit.

liaison.notes: Palestinian side of medical coordination. Phones a number that rarely answers.

amal.notes: Lawyer. Explains what can and cannot be appealed, which is mostly cannot.

bridge.notes: Allenby. Keeps the passport and does not say for how long.

doyle.notes: US preclearance at Pearson. Says 'random' on every flight.

system.notes: Automated text: emails, signs, recorded announcements, printed forms.

nodes.title: Nowruz
nodes.sum: The year turns at the equinox, to the minute. The haft-sin laid out with seven things beginning with the same letter - sabzeh for rebirth, samanu for plenty, senjed for love, seer for health, seeb for beauty, somaq for the victory of good, serkeh for patience.

nodes.title: Chaharshanbe Suri
nodes.sum: Fires in the street on the last Wednesday eve before the new year. Jumping the flame and chanting the line about giving it your winter pallor and taking its red - a Zoroastrian inheritance turned into a street party.

nodes.title: Shab-e Yalda
nodes.sum: The longest night, spent deliberately awake. Pomegranate and watermelon for the red of dawn, the korsi to sit under, and Hafez opened at random to be read as a fortune.

nodes.title: Sizdah Bedar
nodes.sum: The thirteenth day, spent outdoors on principle. The sabzeh from the haft-sin thrown into running water, and everybody in the country apparently in the same park.

nodes.title: An owambe
nodes.sum: It is happening there, and everyone is going. Aso ebi so the family is visibly one family, gele that took someone forty minutes, jollof that will be judged, and money sprayed over the dancers because prosperity is meant to be seen.

nodes.title: A naming ceremony
nodes.sum: Ikomojade - the child stepping forward. The symbolic tastes touched to the child's lips, honey and salt and kola, then the names announced, each one carrying an instruction for the life.

nodes.title: A traditional wedding with two outfits
nodes.sum: The traditional one and the white one, and both are real. Two ceremonies, two guest lists, two sets of photographs, and an argument about the budget that will be retold for thirty years.

nodes.title: Christmas back in the village
nodes.sum: The whole city empties in the third week of December. The road out is a twelve-hour crawl and everyone does it anyway.

nodes.title: The olive harvest
nodes.sum: Mawsim al-zaytoun, from October, the whole family in the grove. Sheets under the trees, singing, bread with oil and za'atar eaten standing up, and a grandmother directing operations from a chair.

nodes.title: A sahra before a wedding
nodes.sum: The evening party at the groom's family's house. The groom shaved in front of everybody to cheering, henna on the hands, and the singing going until it is properly late.

nodes.title: The zaffe
nodes.sum: The wedding procession, with drums. Zaghareet from the women, the drummers walking the couple in, and the line for dabke forming before anyone has decided to dance.

nodes.title: Dabke at a wedding
nodes.sum: The line forms and you are in it. A lawih setting the pace at the front, the Karadiyya loop that lets people join without knowing it, and somebody's uncle who is far better at this than expected.

nodes.title: Eid after the fast
nodes.sum: New clothes, and food in the middle of the day. The first daylight meal in a month, and children given money by everyone they are related to.

nodes.title: Thanksgiving
nodes.sum: A meal with an argument built into the design. Too much food, one relative who says the thing, and leftovers that are better than the meal.

nodes.title: Fourth of July in a yard

nodes.title: A graduation

nodes.title: 925 obstacles between you and everywhere
nodes.sum: Movement inside the West Bank is not a road network with some checkpoints on it. It is an obstacle regime that OCHA counts, item by item, and the count has been rising for three years.

nodes.title: Applying for permission to move inside your own territory
nodes.sum: The permit is the master mechanism. It is discretionary, time-limited, purpose-bound, secret in its criteria, and can be refused by silence rather than by refusal.

nodes.title: The flying checkpoint: an obstacle with no location
nodes.sum: A staffed checkpoint can at least be routed around. A flying checkpoint is erected without notice on any road at any hour, which means no route is ever reliable and no journey can be planned.

nodes.title: The colour of your number plate decides which roads exist
nodes.sum: The road regime runs on vehicle registration, not on identity documents. A Palestinian-plated car is barred from roads that an Israeli-plated car uses freely, and the rule has never been written down.

nodes.title: Area C: 60% of the West Bank you may cross but not use
nodes.sum: The Oslo division was meant to be transitional. Three decades on it is the planning regime, and the largest of the three areas is the one where Palestinian building, farming and infrastructure are effectively prohibited.

nodes.title: There is no airport, and the one nearby is closed to you
nodes.sum: Gaza's airport was destroyed in 2002. Ben Gurion is an hour from Ramallah and West Bank Palestinians are barred from using it. The only way out is through Jordan.

nodes.title: Allenby: the single gateway, and what happens when it shuts
nodes.sum: One crossing carries the entire outbound movement of the West Bank. A single point of failure is not a design flaw here; it is the design.

nodes.title: Rafah, and the price of a place in the queue
nodes.sum: Gaza's crossing to Egypt has operated intermittently for two decades. When it opens, access to it is rationed - and the rationing has a price list.

nodes.title: Being refused entry to the place you are from
nodes.sum: Return is not guaranteed. For a Palestinian abroad, going home is an application, and a refusal at the bridge is not appealable from outside.

nodes.title: Israel holds the registry that says you exist
nodes.sum: The Palestinian population registry is controlled by Israel. Births, marriages, divorces, deaths and address changes all require Israeli approval before the Palestinian Authority may issue or amend an ID.

nodes.title: Green ID, blue ID, and what each one forbids
nodes.sum: Which document you hold is mostly an accident of where a relative was standing in 1967. It determines which roads, cities, hospitals and countries are available to you for the rest of your life.

nodes.title: Jerusalem residency as a privilege that can be withdrawn
nodes.sum: East Jerusalem Palestinians were made permanent residents, not citizens. Permanent residency is revocable, and the criteria for revoking it were widened after the fact.

nodes.title: Registered in Gaza, living in the West Bank: illegal at home
nodes.sum: Since 2000 Israel has refused to let Gaza-registered Palestinians change their ID address to the West Bank. People born and raised in the West Bank are classified as illegal aliens in it.

nodes.title: A passport that is a travel document, not a nationality
nodes.sum: The Palestinian Authority passport is accepted by many states as a travel document while conferring none of the things a nationality confers, because the issuing authority is not a state those countries recognise.

nodes.title: Statelessness, inherited
nodes.sum: Refugee status passes down the generations, and most host states have deliberately not naturalised the people living in them for seventy years. The condition is heritable and the number therefore only grows.

nodes.title: The document with no national number
nodes.sum: Jordan's ex-Gaza Palestinians hold a travel document that looks like a passport, functions as a residence permit, expires every two years, and is refused by several of the countries it would most be used for.

nodes.title: Naturalising abroad, and the political test attached
nodes.sum: In some states the route out of statelessness now carries a declaration about the conflict itself, which converts a citizenship application into a test of political opinion.

nodes.title: The building permit that is not issued
nodes.sum: Building legally in Area C requires a permit from the Israeli Civil Administration. The approval rate is close to zero and has been for twenty-five years, which means every Palestinian home built there is unlawful by construction.

nodes.title: Demolition, at 4.7 structures a day
nodes.sum: Demolition for want of a permit is not an occasional event. It runs at a measured daily rate and the rate is rising.

nodes.title: Punitive demolition: the family pays for the accused
nodes.sum: Separately from permit demolitions, homes are demolished as punishment for an attack allegedly committed by a family member - frequently before any trial, and always against people not accused of anything.

nodes.title: Settler violence at five incidents a day
nodes.sum: Attacks by settlers on Palestinian people and property reached the highest levels OCHA has recorded since it began counting in 2006, and the UN human rights office finds they occur with the acquiescence or participation of security forces.

nodes.title: The olive harvest, and being let onto your own land for one day
nodes.sum: The harvest is both the agricultural year and the cultural one. It now runs under a coordination regime that grants access late, briefly, and to a fraction of the land.

nodes.title: Impunity, and what it does to the arithmetic
nodes.sum: Where attacks are rarely prosecuted, the cost-benefit facing both the attacker and the victim changes permanently, and the victim's rational response looks from outside like passivity.

nodes.title: Administrative detention: held on material you cannot see
nodes.sum: Detention without charge or trial, on secret evidence, for renewable six-month periods with no limit on renewals. There is no allegation to answer because none is made.

nodes.title: A court system with a conviction rate above 99%
nodes.sum: West Bank Palestinians are tried by military courts. The conviction rate is such that the trial is not meaningfully a contest, and every strategy is built around plea rather than defence.

nodes.title: Women in detention
nodes.sum: Women detainees face the general conditions plus a set of specific ones - strip searches, menstrual management with no supplies, and the certainty that detention itself will follow them socially afterwards.

nodes.title: No conjugal visits, and what people did about it
nodes.sum: Israel does not grant conjugal visits to Palestinian security prisoners. The response - smuggling sperm out for IVF - is one of the strangest and best-documented adaptations in this dataset, and the state has moved against the children it produced.

nodes.title: The medical permit, and the difference between denial and silence
nodes.sum: Specialist care is largely outside Gaza and outside the West Bank's reach, so treatment requires an exit permit. The permit is rarely refused outright; it is more often simply not answered before the appointment passes.

nodes.title: Travelling to treatment alone
nodes.sum: A patient may be approved while the person who would accompany her is not. For children, the elderly and women travelling to unfamiliar cities, the companion permit is the one that decides whether the journey happens.

nodes.title: Which illness you have decides your odds at the window
nodes.sum: Approval rates vary substantially by medical specialty, which means the permit system performs a form of triage that no clinician designed and no patient is told about.

nodes.title: Evacuation as the only remaining option
nodes.sum: Where the health system is destroyed rather than merely restricted, treatment means leaving the territory entirely - a process with a small quota, a closed crossing and no return guarantee.

nodes.title: Giving birth at a checkpoint
nodes.sum: The most documented single intersection of occupation and gender. Labour does not wait for a gate to open, and the road between a village and a maternity ward has soldiers on it.

nodes.title: Two authorities, one journey: the guardian rule on top of the permit
nodes.sum: A Palestinian woman in Gaza needs Israel's permission to leave and, since 2021, may be stopped by a male relative's application to a court. Either alone would be a hurdle; together they are a trap with two keys and she holds neither.

nodes.title: Personal status law: two territories, two codes, neither written here
nodes.sum: Family law in the West Bank is Jordanian, in Gaza it is Egyptian, and both predate the Palestinian Authority. A woman's rights in marriage, divorce, custody and inheritance depend on which occupation-era statute her postcode inherited.

nodes.title: The killing that gets a reduced sentence
nodes.sum: The provision granting a pardoning excuse for so-called honour killings was annulled in 2011. The articles that reduce the sentence anyway were not, and the courts continue to use them.

nodes.title: Managing a period when there is nothing to manage it with
nodes.sum: Under siege and displacement, menstruation becomes a logistics problem with no supplies, no privacy, no water and no disposal - and the coping strategy that emerged is pharmacological.

nodes.title: Being pregnant while it is happening
nodes.sum: Pregnancy does not pause for a war. Where the health system has collapsed, the ordinary complications become fatal and the ordinary procedures are performed without anaesthesia.

nodes.title: Early marriage, and the reasons that are not tradition
nodes.sum: Marriage ages are set at 18 in the West Bank and 17 in Gaza and can be lowered by a judge with a guardian's approval. Where movement, education and income are all constrained, marriage becomes the available route and the constraint is read afterwards as culture.

nodes.title: The family unification freeze
nodes.sum: Since 2002 Israelis and Jerusalem residents have been barred from obtaining status for a Palestinian spouse from the occupied territory. The measure was temporary in 2002 and is still in force.

nodes.title: Living together illegally in your own country
nodes.sum: Where the registry will not align two spouses' addresses, the family lives together in breach of the rules, in constant exposure to detention and forcible transfer.

nodes.title: Visiting someone in prison
nodes.sum: Prison visits require a permit, a route through several checkpoints, an entire day, and frequently end in refusal at the last gate. The person doing this is almost always a woman.

nodes.title: The family spread across four jurisdictions
nodes.sum: An ordinary extended family may hold West Bank, Gaza, Jerusalem, Israeli and diaspora documents. No single event - a wedding, a funeral, an anniversary - can lawfully be attended by all of them.

nodes.title: The university as a target
nodes.sum: Palestinian universities are raided, their students detained in numbers, and UN experts describe this as systematic policy rather than episodic violence.

nodes.title: Winning the scholarship and not being able to take it
nodes.sum: Admission is the easy part. The visa, the exit permit, the guardian's consent and the crossing all have to align, and each is separately capable of ending it.

nodes.title: A qualification from a place the world is unsure about
nodes.sum: Credential recognition assumes a stable issuing authority, an archive that can be written to, and a postal route. Where those are damaged, a real degree becomes unprovable.

nodes.title: A work permit tied to one employer
nodes.sum: The permit is issued in an Israeli employer's name after an army security clearance. It binds the worker to that employer, that area and a curfew, which is the structural cause of everything in WRK-002.

nodes.title: The broker who sells you your own permit
nodes.sum: A permit bound to one employer and issued in scarce quantities produces a black market. It is large, measured by Israel's own central bank, and the worker pays for it out of the wage the permit lets him earn.

nodes.title: Wage theft that cannot be reported
nodes.sum: Where the intermediary collects the wage, the worker often does not know who the employer legally is - which makes every labour protection unusable.

nodes.title: Women's work, and why the participation rate is what it is
nodes.sum: Female labour force participation is very low, and the usual explanation is culture. The mechanical explanations - checkpoints, childcare, permit exclusion and safety - come first.

nodes.title: PayPal serves the settlement and not the village
nodes.sum: The clearest single example of digital exclusion drawn along national lines rather than geographic ones: the same territory, two populations, one of which has payment services.

nodes.title: Freelancing with no way to be paid
nodes.sum: Remote work is the obvious answer to a closed border. The payment layer is where it fails, and the failure is expensive rather than absolute.

nodes.title: Compliance as a permanent surcharge
nodes.sum: For Palestinians abroad, financial life is not blocked so much as taxed - additional checks, delays, refused products and worse rates, indefinitely.

nodes.title: An economy with somebody else's currency and customs
nodes.sum: The Palestinian economy uses the shekel, and its import duties and VAT are collected by Israel and remitted - or withheld - as a political instrument.

nodes.title: Held on 2G by spectrum allocation
nodes.sum: Israel controls frequency allocation under the Oslo framework. Palestinian operators got a sliver of spectrum in 1999 and kept it while their subscriber base multiplied twentyfold.

nodes.title: The blackout as an instrument
nodes.sum: Connectivity can be cut, and when it is, it removes the ability to call an ambulance, reach family, verify a rumour or document anything.

nodes.title: Being surveilled as the default condition
nodes.sum: Phone, movement, social media and facial recognition data are collected at a density that changes what people are willing to say and where they are willing to go.

nodes.title: Water that is not drinkable
nodes.sum: Gaza's only natural water source has been over-pumped and contaminated to the point where almost none of it is fit to drink, and the fixes require imports that the closure restricts.

nodes.title: Electricity by the hour
nodes.sum: A chronic deficit means power arrives in blocks and everything - study, refrigeration, medical equipment, water pumping - is scheduled around it.

nodes.title: Fishing inside a line drawn offshore
nodes.sum: The fishing zone agreed at Oslo was 20 nautical miles. The enforced limit has been a fraction of that, which converts a fishing industry into a subsistence one.

nodes.title: The list of things you may not import
nodes.sum: The clearest documented absurdity in the whole file: for three years almost everything was banned unless specifically permitted, and the permitted list was never published.

nodes.title: Being blamed for the conditions the siege produced
nodes.sum: Unemployment, aid dependency and a weak private sector are read abroad as evidence about Palestinians rather than as the measured outputs of a closure policy.

nodes.title: Thirty-nine professions you may not enter
nodes.sum: In Lebanon, Palestinian refugees are barred from dozens of syndicated professions. The bar is not on ability or qualification; it is on the category the person was born into.

nodes.title: Not being allowed to own the home you live in
nodes.sum: Lebanon's 2001 property law bars Palestinians from owning real estate, using a formula that never names them.

nodes.title: A status you inherit and cannot exit
nodes.sum: Host states have largely declined naturalisation as a matter of policy, and the status passes to children, so the condition compounds rather than resolving.

nodes.title: Being refused as a refugee, again
nodes.sum: When displacement recurs, the neighbouring states publicly refuse to receive the displaced - which is itself a message received by the people being bombed.

nodes.title: A database built to stop you being employed
nodes.sum: Doxxing operations publish profiles of students and academics with the explicitly stated purpose of preventing their future employment, and internally track firings as a performance metric.

nodes.title: Being the designated explainer
nodes.sum: During any escalation, every colleague and acquaintance treats the nearest Palestinian as a spokesperson, an explanation service or a proxy defendant.

nodes.title: The cost of a name on a CV
nodes.sum: Before any speech, the name alone does work in a hiring process, a tenancy application and a security clearance.

nodes.title: Sending money back, and what it takes
nodes.sum: Remittance is the mechanism through which obligation, guilt and power are negotiated in a family split by a border - and the payment rails make it expensive and legally exposed.

nodes.title: The watchlist, and whose names are on it
nodes.sum: Airport screening in the US runs on name-based watchlist matching. The best available analysis of the list's composition indicates it is overwhelmingly Muslim names, which makes 'random' additional screening statistically anything but.

nodes.title: Held at the border with a valid visa
nodes.sum: A visa is permission to travel to a port of entry, not to enter. Recent cases show Palestinians with valid documents held for days, without counsel, with no reason given.

nodes.title: Redress that does not redress
nodes.sum: The official remedy for repeated wrongful screening is a complaint programme whose effectiveness is contested by the people who use it and by government auditors.

nodes.title: The exit interview at your own departure
nodes.sum: Departing from Ben Gurion - for those few permitted - and from several regional airports involves an interrogation calibrated to origin, conducted in public, with luggage opened in front of the queue.

nodes.title: A name with no correct spelling
nodes.sum: Arabic names have no single canonical Latin transliteration, so the same person's name is legitimately spelled several ways across her own documents - and every system that compares documents treats that as a discrepancy.

nodes.title: The identity is frozen before you reach the airport
nodes.sum: Modern air travel locks a vetted identity at booking. A mismatch discovered later cannot be corrected at the gate, by anyone, for technical reasons.

nodes.title: Being mistaken for someone
nodes.sum: A false positive against a watchlist or a sanctions list is not a brief inconvenience; it attaches to the person and reappears at every subsequent check.

nodes.title: The officer who decided, and the one who would not have
nodes.sum: A large share of these hurdles are not policy. They are one person's decision on one day, which another person on another day would have made differently - and which is then permanent.

nodes.title: The clerical error that becomes your permanent record
nodes.sum: A wrong date, a wrong spelling, a wrong status code entered once is copied forward by every subsequent system, and the burden of disproving it is entirely the person's.

nodes.title: The letterhead
nodes.sum: The single most concise illustration in this dataset of bureaucracy as an instrument: a document about a dying man was refused because of the words printed at the top of it.

nodes.title: Being read as a threat before you speak
nodes.sum: The identity arrives in the room first and carries a prepackaged meaning assembled by decades of coverage. Everything after that is spent correcting an impression nobody admits to having.

nodes.title: The marriage and relationship market, with the identity priced in
nodes.sum: The user's brief names this directly and it is real: the identity changes who will partner with you, on what terms, and how the relationship is read by everyone around it - in both directions, at home and abroad.

nodes.title: Learning to say nothing
nodes.sum: Where speech carries permit, employment, visa and naturalisation consequences, silence is the rational strategy - and practising it for years does specific damage.

nodes.title: Threat that does not end, so there is no 'post'
nodes.sum: Trauma frameworks assume the event has finished. Under an ongoing occupation the hypervigilance is an accurate reading of the present, which makes most of the treatment literature inapplicable.

nodes.title: Waiting, as a permanent condition
nodes.sum: Almost every hurdle in this dataset resolves into waiting for a decision by someone who owes no answer and keeps no deadline. Sustained uncertainty is a distinct injury from bad news.

nodes.title: What it takes out of the work
nodes.sum: The brief asks specifically for the effects on efficiency and growth. They are real, they are large, and they are attributed to the person rather than the conditions in essentially every setting.

nodes.title: Back pain, and the fact that it is measured
nodes.sum: The brief asks about back pain specifically. It is not a figure of speech: somatic symptom disorder has a published prevalence in Palestinian primary care, back pain is the second commonest presentation, and being female roughly doubles the odds.

nodes.title: Chronic pain, with the psychological load measured alongside it
nodes.sum: A Gaza hospital study puts numbers on the combination the rest of this dataset describes: long-duration pain, near-universal psychological distress, and poverty, in the same patients.

nodes.title: Stressful working conditions, and the back that carries them
nodes.sum: The link between the conditions and the body has been measured in the occupational literature too, in the workforce that holds the health system together.

nodes.title: The productivity loss nobody has quantified
nodes.sum: The brief asks about effects on efficiency and growth. The honest position is that the mechanism is well evidenced and the magnitude is not, because the study has not been done.

nodes.title: Detaining the doctors and nurses
nodes.sum: Medical workers have been detained in numbers, held without charge for very long periods, and - according to multiple monitoring bodies - tortured. The interrogations reportedly concerned their hospitals and colleagues rather than any alleged offence.

nodes.title: Dying in custody
nodes.sum: The Special Rapporteur on torture records deaths in custody in numbers, with a stated lack of transparency about causes. The most documented individual case is a surgeon who was never charged with anything.

nodes.title: Sexual and gender-based violence in detention, found to be policy
nodes.sum: The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that sexual, reproductive and other gender-based violence against Palestinian detainees was not incidental but an intentional policy forming part of standard operating procedures.

nodes.title: Attacking the health system itself
nodes.sum: Beyond individual detentions, monitoring bodies record sustained attacks on hospitals, ambulances and health workers at a scale UN experts have described as 'medicide'.

nodes.title: Atrocities against civilians, and the problem of the record
nodes.sum: Beyond detention, monitoring bodies document killings, enforced disappearances and starvation as method. The specific hurdle recorded here is that the documentation is obstructed, so the record will always understate it.

nodes.title: At the moment of travel, the nationality does not exist
nodes.sum: The brief asks for this specifically. It is not that the passport is weak - it is that in the systems that actually move people across borders, the country is frequently not an option that can be selected.

nodes.title: Travelling on a document whose nationality field says 'Undefined'
nodes.sum: East Jerusalem Palestinians mostly hold no passport at all. They travel on an Israeli laissez-passer that confers no nationality, states the holder's nationality as undefined, and carries a re-entry permit that can be forfeited.

nodes.title: Proving who you are, again
nodes.sum: Every institution verifies you separately, none of them trust each other's verification, and each wants a different combination of documents you must locate, copy and produce in person.

nodes.title: The renewal treadmill
nodes.sum: Passport, licence, registration, insurance, membership, subscription, permit. Each has its own cycle and its own portal, so something is always about to lapse and the lapse is always your fault.

nodes.title: Open when you are at work
nodes.sum: Offices, clinics, banks and tradespeople operate during working hours, so accessing them costs annual leave or lost pay.

nodes.title: Hold music, and the person who cannot help you
nodes.sum: Support lines are built around cost per call. The person who answers can read the screen and rarely change what is on it.

nodes.title: The typo that becomes official
nodes.sum: One wrong character in a name, date, address or account number propagates into every system downstream, and correcting it is always harder than making it.

nodes.title: Their mistake, your problem
nodes.sum: Institutions presume their own records are correct. When they are not, discovering it, proving it and fixing it is entirely the work of the person harmed.

nodes.title: Mistaken for someone else
nodes.sum: Matching is fuzzy. A similar name, a shared birth date or a recycled phone number attaches another person's record - debts, fines, medical history - to you, and disproving it is your job.

nodes.title: After the crash
nodes.sum: The collision takes four seconds. What follows is months of insurers, assessors, hire cars, medical appointments and an argument about liability you did not want to have.

nodes.title: The ordinary injury
nodes.sum: A fall, a ladder, a kitchen, a football pitch, ice. The healing is the easy part; the hard part is doing your job and your life at reduced capacity while nobody adjusts anything.

nodes.title: You get ill, and nobody decided it
nodes.sum: Cancer, autoimmune disease, a cardiac event, a neurological condition. No behaviour reliably prevents them, no one is responsible, and the diagnosis reorganises everything around it.

nodes.title: The waiting list
nodes.sum: Where care is rationed by queue rather than price, the wait is assigned to you without negotiation and without a date you can plan around.

nodes.title: The illness generates an invoice
nodes.sum: In systems that bill individuals, a medical event produces a bill nobody quoted in advance, for an amount nobody can state beforehand, from providers you did not choose.

nodes.title: Cover attached to a job
nodes.sum: Where health cover comes through an employer, losing or changing work removes medical care at the same moment it removes income - and staying in a bad job becomes a medical decision.

nodes.title: The body slows on a timetable you do not set
nodes.sum: Recovery lengthens, sleep degrades, eyesight goes, strength declines. Gradual enough to be invisible, cumulative enough to be decisive, entirely non-negotiable.

nodes.title: Being burgled or robbed
nodes.sum: Someone decides to take your things. The loss is the smallest part; the aftermath is locksmiths, insurers, reference numbers, and not feeling right in your own rooms.

nodes.title: On the receiving end of someone else's driving
nodes.sum: Another person's speed, phone or inattention arrives in your life at a junction, and everything that follows is yours to administer.

nodes.title: Where you live decides which disaster you get
nodes.sum: Flood, wildfire, hurricane, earthquake, heatwave, freeze. The exposure comes with the ground, and the ground came with the job, the family or the price.

nodes.title: Someone is trying to defraud you, professionally
nodes.sum: Calls, texts, emails and messages engineered by people who do this full time, arriving whether or not you engage with anything.

nodes.title: Your data was lost by someone you never dealt with
nodes.sum: Organisations you have no relationship with hold records about you and lose them. Nothing you did caused it and nothing you can do fixes it.

nodes.title: The job ends because someone else did arithmetic
nodes.sum: Layoffs, restructures, acquisitions and closures arrive on a timetable set elsewhere. The decision is about headcount and cost centres, not about you, and the income stops anyway.

nodes.title: The manager you were assigned
nodes.sum: Whether a job is tolerable is largely one person, allocated to you, who can change without notice and without any change to your contract.

nodes.title: Working while ill, because the alternative is worse
nodes.sum: Where sick pay is thin or absent, illness becomes a financial calculation, and the calculation usually says go in.

nodes.title: Your largest expense is set annually by someone else
nodes.sum: For renters, the price of having somewhere to live is decided by another party once a year, and the only counter-move costs more than accepting it.

nodes.title: Things break, and they break together
nodes.sum: Boiler, roof, car, washing machine, phone. Each has a lifespan, they were often bought at the same time, and they fail at whatever moment they fail at.

nodes.title: Someone will need looking after
nodes.sum: An ageing parent, a sick partner, a child with additional needs. It arrives unscheduled, lasts years, is unpaid, and lands on whoever is nearest or least able to refuse.

nodes.title: Bereavement, and the paperwork of it
nodes.sum: Grief arrives with an administrative workload - registration, probate, accounts, utilities, pensions - executed by the person least able to concentrate.

nodes.title: Locked out of your own account
nodes.sum: Identity online is a chain of recovery methods. Break one link - a dead number, a lost authenticator, a closed email - and the chain does not reconnect.

nodes.title: The thing you relied on is discontinued
nodes.sum: Services close, formats are abandoned, apps are bought and shut, devices stop receiving updates. The decision is a company's; the migration is yours.

nodes.title: You must have a car, because of how the place was built
nodes.sum: Where there is no viable transit, car ownership is not a preference - it is a condition of employment, imposed by planning decisions made before you arrived.

nodes.title: The commute
nodes.sum: A daily journey is the largest recurring involuntary time cost most working people carry. It is unpaid, not counted as work, and mostly set by where housing is affordable.

nodes.title: The credential you must hold to be considered
nodes.sum: Employers set entry requirements. Roles that once needed a school certificate now need a degree, without a corresponding change in the work - so the qualification is a toll, not a choice.

nodes.title: The structures that made friends are removed
nodes.sum: School, university and early jobs supply repeated unplanned contact. Adult life does not, so friendship becomes something that must be organised or it ends.

nodes.title: You cannot afford to enforce your own rights
nodes.sum: Most everyday legal wrongs are worth less than the cost of pursuing them, so the right exists and the remedy does not - and the other party knows it.

nodes.title: Compelled participation
nodes.sum: Jury service, tax filing, census, registration, court witness summons. Duties that take real time, are not optional, and are scheduled by the state.

nodes.title: Everything you have requires upkeep
nodes.sum: Possessions, accounts, documents, health and qualifications all decay without input. The work returns you to baseline; none of it is progress.

nodes.title: The queue
nodes.sum: Waiting is allocated to you by whoever is providing the thing, in units they do not pay for and you cannot spend elsewhere.

nodes.title: You were born into a cohort and the cohort has a price
nodes.sum: House prices, interest rates, the labour market in your graduation year, whether a pandemic falls in your twenties. None is chosen, and all of it compounds.

nodes.title: The volume of small compulsory decisions
nodes.sum: Tariffs, plans, policies, renewals and options all require comparison. The choosing is imposed; the alternative is paying the default price.

nodes.title: Ambient activation that never resolves
nodes.sum: News, notifications and always-on messaging produce a baseline of alertness nobody opted into, and it does not switch off because the devices do not.

nodes.title: The night, and what the body learns in it
nodes.sum: Bombardment happens mostly at night, which means the damage is done to a nervous system that is supposed to be asleep. The body learns, within about three nights, that darkness is when it must be awake.

nodes.title: Sirens, alerts, and the phone that decides your pulse
nodes.sum: Warning systems save lives and condition the population at the same time. The alert tone becomes a stimulus that produces a physical reaction independent of whether anything follows it.

nodes.title: The interruption of everything at once
nodes.sum: War does not damage one thing. School, work, transport, banking, medicine, post and the electricity that runs them all stop in the same week, so there is no functioning system left to fall back on.

nodes.title: Decision-making under a threat that will not resolve
nodes.sum: Stay or go, now or tomorrow, this road or that one. The information needed to decide does not exist, the consequences are irreversible, and the decisions arrive faster than anyone can process them.

nodes.title: Leaving with what you can carry
nodes.sum: Displacement is usually described as a movement. Psychologically it is a forced triage of an entire life into one bag, performed in under an hour, with no possibility of revision.

nodes.title: The internal displacement nobody counts
nodes.sum: Most people displaced by war never cross a border. They move to a cousin's flat in another city, which involves no agency, no registration and no support, and puts two families under strain instead of one.

nodes.title: Being unable to flee at all
nodes.sum: The people who leave are the ones with money, documents, a car and somewhere to go. Everybody else stays, and knows precisely why they stayed.

nodes.title: Death without a funeral
nodes.sum: Grief in peacetime has a procedure: a body, a burial, a gathering, a period. War removes all four, and the mind does not process a loss it was never given the ritual for.

nodes.title: Losing several people at once
nodes.sum: Bereavement services and the mind itself are built for one loss at a time. War delivers them in batches, and the second loss interrupts the processing of the first, and so on.

nodes.title: Grieving from four thousand kilometres away
nodes.sum: Being abroad when someone dies at home removes every mechanism grief uses: the body, the house, the people, the food, the physical presence of others who also loved them.

nodes.title: The blackout
nodes.sum: Cutting a population's connectivity is a weapon used on both sides of a border at once: it isolates the people inside and it terrorises the people outside who cannot reach them.

nodes.title: Being lied to by everybody, on purpose
nodes.sum: Every party to a modern conflict runs an information operation aimed at the civilian population. The effect on an individual is the removal of any reliable basis for deciding what to do.

nodes.title: Watching your own city on a stranger's timeline
nodes.sum: The war arrives as an infinite feed of graphic content about specific streets the viewer knows, interleaved with advertising and other people's holidays.

nodes.title: PTSD, as it actually presents
nodes.sum: The diagnosis is well known and the presentation is not. It is mostly not flashbacks; it is sleep, irritability, concentration, numbness, and an avoidance pattern the person has rationalised so thoroughly they no longer notices it.

nodes.title: Continuous traumatic stress: when there is no 'post'
nodes.sum: PTSD assumes the trauma has ended. For a population under ongoing or recurring threat it has not, which makes hypervigilance a correct assessment of reality rather than a symptom to be treated.

nodes.title: The body keeps the bill: physical health after war stress
nodes.sum: Chronic threat exposure is not confined to the mind. It shows up as cardiovascular disease, metabolic change, immune dysfunction and pain, on a delay of ten to thirty years.

nodes.title: Not being able to describe it, in any language
nodes.sum: Recovery frameworks are built on the assumption that the experience can be narrated. A large part of war exposure is encoded as sensation, not story, and the person has no words for it in their first language, let alone their third.

nodes.title: Survivor guilt, in its specific forms
nodes.sum: Not a vague sadness. A set of concrete, recurring propositions - I took the seat, I did not go back, I was asleep - each of which the person has examined thousands of times and cannot dismiss.

nodes.title: Moral injury: doing, or failing to do
nodes.sum: Distinct from fear-based trauma. Moral injury is the damage from having acted, or failed to act, against one's own code - and it responds poorly to treatments designed for fear.

nodes.title: Rage at your own side
nodes.sum: One of the least discussed effects. Civilians under bombardment frequently direct their strongest anger not at the attacker but at their own authorities, for the shelter that was not built and the warning that did not come.

nodes.title: Development does not pause for the war
nodes.sum: An adult loses time. A child loses a stage. Language, attachment, literacy and social learning run on windows, and a window missed is not reopened by the conflict ending.

nodes.title: Growing up with a parent who is not fully present
nodes.sum: The child of a war-injured parent is not a bystander. Parental PTSD changes the emotional climate of the household every day for the whole of a childhood.

nodes.title: Children with no schooling system to return to
nodes.sum: The institutions are not merely closed. Teachers are displaced or dead, buildings are rubble or shelter, records are destroyed, and the qualification a child needs proof of has no issuing authority left.

nodes.title: Play, and what replaces it
nodes.sum: Children process the unmanageable through play, and under war the play becomes re-enactment: checkpoints, funerals, bombing. Adults find it disturbing and stop it, which removes the only processing mechanism the child has.

nodes.title: Prenatal stress and neurodevelopmental risk
nodes.sum: Exposure begins before birth. Maternal stress during pregnancy is associated with elevated risk of ASD and ADHD in the offspring - elevated, not determined, and the distinction is the whole of the honest version.

nodes.title: Famine and deprivation in utero
nodes.sum: Siege and blockade produce maternal malnutrition, and the best-documented prenatal exposure in all of human epidemiology is a famine caused by a war.

nodes.title: Blast, toxicants and the developing brain
nodes.sum: Beyond stress: war deposits heavy metals, combustion products and munition residues into the air, water and soil that a child is growing in.

nodes.title: Sulfur mustard: the exposure that keeps arriving
nodes.sum: Mustard gas has low mortality and very high morbidity. Its defining feature is latency: the eye, lung and skin damage that disables a survivor often appears fifteen to twenty years after an attack they thought they had survived.

nodes.title: Halabja: gas used on a town
nodes.sum: The largest chemical attack on a civilian-populated area in history, and the best long-run evidence available for what that does to a population and to the generations after it.

nodes.title: Living with an exposure you cannot prove
nodes.sum: Compensation, treatment and recognition all require documentation of exposure. Chemical attacks are not administered with receipts, and the people who could confirm it are frequently dead.

nodes.title: What healing actually looks like, chemically
nodes.sum: There is no cure for sulfur mustard injury. Management is symptomatic, lifelong and progressive, and the honest clinical framing is slowing a decline rather than recovering from an event.

nodes.title: Hearing, after blast
nodes.sum: Tinnitus and hearing loss are among the commonest consequences of blast exposure, and a normal audiogram does not rule out a functional deficit.

nodes.title: Sight, smell and the senses that carry the memory
nodes.sum: Vision loss after blast and gas is well documented. Smell is the one nobody treats and the one that reactivates everything.

nodes.title: Blast traumatic brain injury without a visible head injury
nodes.sum: Overpressure injures the brain without impact. A person with no wound, no loss of consciousness and a normal scan can have chronic post-concussive symptoms for fifteen years and more.

nodes.title: Amputation and the life built around it
nodes.sum: A prosthesis is not a solution, it is a subscription. Sockets need refitting, components wear out, children outgrow limbs every year, and all of it must be paid for in a country whose supply chain is under sanction.

nodes.title: Psychiatric disability, and the fact that it is a disability
nodes.sum: Severe, chronic war-related psychiatric illness is disabling in exactly the way a physical injury is, and is treated by almost every system - medical, legal, familial - as something the person could stop doing.

nodes.title: Being disabled in a country that was damaged too
nodes.sum: Disability is produced by the interaction of an impairment with an environment. War damages the environment at the same time as it produces the impairment, so the same injury is far more disabling than it would be elsewhere.

nodes.title: There is no mental health system left
nodes.sum: The collapse of services is simultaneous with the surge in need. The population most requiring psychiatric care is in the place where psychiatric care has just been destroyed.

nodes.title: Being treated abroad, by people with no reference for it
nodes.sum: Resettled survivors reach functioning health systems and encounter clinicians with no framework for the event, no shared language and a fifty-minute appointment.

nodes.title: What recovery actually means, and what it does not
nodes.sum: Some of this resolves. Some of it becomes manageable. Some of it is permanent. Treating all three as the same category is how both patients and clinicians end up feeling they have failed.

nodes.title: Being attacked as a category rather than an individual
nodes.sum: Ordinary war damage is impersonal - you were in the wrong place. Genocidal violence is the opposite: it is precisely about who you are, and that changes what the survivor concludes about themselves.

nodes.title: Sexual violence as a weapon, and the silence around it
nodes.sum: Mass sexual violence is a standard instrument of genocidal and ethnic campaigns, and it is the one category of war injury that the victim's own community most reliably punishes them for.

nodes.title: Erasure: when the place stops being yours
nodes.sum: Renamed streets, demolished cemeteries, rewritten curricula, a new population in the same houses. The survivor's memory becomes officially incorrect.

nodes.title: A war with no explosion and the same casualties
nodes.sum: Comprehensive sanctions are an instrument of war aimed at a civilian population. They produce mortality, disability and psychiatric illness through the health system, the supply chain and the currency instead of through ordnance.

nodes.title: Domestic production struck as well
nodes.sum: Where sanctions are combined with kinetic strikes on pharmaceutical and medical manufacturing, the substitution route that made the sanctions survivable is removed at the same time.

nodes.title: Sanctions as a planning-horizon weapon
nodes.sum: The most durable psychological effect of long-running economic war is the removal of the future as a usable concept. Nobody can plan five years ahead, so nobody does, and the behaviour that produces is then blamed on the culture.

nodes.title: Mental health care under economic war
nodes.sum: Psychiatric medicine is import-dependent, psychotherapy is unaffordable at a collapsed exchange rate, and the population needing both is the one the sanctions and the war are being applied to.

nodes.title: Hunger as a psychological instrument
nodes.sum: Deliberate deprivation does specific and well-characterised things to cognition and behaviour, and those effects are then presented as evidence about the character of the besieged population.

nodes.title: Water, sewage, and the dignity floor
nodes.sum: The psychological literature on siege focuses on food. Survivors more often describe sanitation - the specific humiliation of having nowhere clean to wash, defecate or menstruate.

nodes.title: The passport as a wall
nodes.sum: A travel document that no one will accept converts the entire world outside the border into a theoretical place. That is a psychological condition, not an administrative one.

nodes.title: Not being able to go back either
nodes.sum: Immobility is symmetrical and the second direction is discussed far less. For many, returning means conscription, an open case, an exit ban, or simply not being certain of getting out again.

nodes.title: Statelessness in practice, if not in law
nodes.sum: Someone whose passport cannot be renewed abroad, whose country's consulate is closed, and whose host country will not regularise them, has all the properties of statelessness without the legal status that comes with protections.

nodes.title: The account closed in a country you are not at war with
nodes.sum: De-risking means a bank in a third country closes an ordinary person's account because of where they were born. It is not a sanction, it is a bank deciding the person is not worth the compliance cost.

nodes.title: Squeezed from both sides at once
nodes.sum: Foreign banks close the account for being Iranian, and the Iranian state freezes assets of citizens abroad it disapproves of. The person is excluded by both jurisdictions simultaneously.

nodes.title: Paying more for everything, permanently
nodes.sum: Financial exclusion is not binary. Most people are not cut off; they are surcharged - worse rates, more checks, more documents, more delays, forever.

nodes.title: Watching money disappear while you hold it
nodes.sum: Hyperinflation is experienced as a continuous small theft. The psychological effect is distinct from poverty: it is the loss of the relationship between effort and reward.

nodes.title: The cost of the war is billed to the household
nodes.sum: Reconstruction, defence and sanctions absorption are all ultimately paid out of household consumption, usually through inflation and subsidy removal rather than through anything a citizen can see or vote on.

nodes.title: The recognised clinical burden of watching from outside
nodes.sum: Distance is protective against blast and not against much else. The diaspora symptom profile is now described in the medical literature as a distinct and under-recognised burden.

nodes.title: Being asked to explain your country at work
nodes.sum: During a war, every colleague, acquaintance and stranger with an opinion treats the nearest person of that nationality as a spokesman, an explanation service, or a proxy defendant.

nodes.title: The family who stayed, and the money
nodes.sum: Remittance is not only an economic transfer. It is the mechanism by which guilt, obligation and power are negotiated inside a family split by a war.

nodes.title: Being the nationality of a war
nodes.sum: When a country is in the news as a threat, everyone carrying its nationality is reclassified abroad - at borders, at work, in the street, and by algorithms.

nodes.title: The community turns on itself
nodes.sum: War splits diaspora communities along lines about the war, and the resulting fracture removes the co-ethnic support network that is the main protective factor available.

nodes.title: How it actually reaches the next generation
nodes.sum: Before any genetics: the primary transmission route is a household. What the child absorbs is the parent's vigilance, silence, anger and rules, delivered daily for eighteen years.

nodes.title: Marriage, intimacy and what does not get said
nodes.sum: War damage lands hardest on the relationship that is meant to be the recovery environment, and the mechanisms by which it does are almost never named in the marriage.

nodes.title: The child who becomes the adult
nodes.sum: Parentification: when the adults are incapacitated, grieving, displaced or non-speakers of the new language, a child takes over the running of the family.

nodes.title: Epigenetic transmission: what the evidence actually says
nodes.sum: The claim that trauma is inherited biologically is partly supported, frequently overstated, and important enough to state precisely rather than loosely.

nodes.title: Transmission without genes at all
nodes.sum: The strongest generational evidence in this dataset is not genetic. Descendants who share no ancestry with the exposed show the same elevated symptoms, which means the mechanism is the society, not the germline.

nodes.title: What descendants actually carry
nodes.sum: The third generation is not a study population. They are people who have particular recurring experiences - and those experiences are specific enough to be listed rather than gestured at.

nodes.title: Physical inheritance: the parent's damaged body
nodes.sum: Some of the generational transfer is neither psychological nor epigenetic. It is that a chemically or radiologically injured parent has children, and the injury is present in the pregnancy.

SC-CHECKPOINT.note: The checkpoint on the way to school, and every journey after it. Cages, turnstiles, a queue that starts before dawn.

SC-PERMIT-WINDOW.note: The District Coordination Office window. Where the tasreeh is applied for, and where the answer is usually nothing at all.

SC-OLIVE-GROVE.note: Terraced olive trees older than every document in this story. The harvest, and the one day a year it is allowed.

SC-ALLENBY.note: The King Hussein bridge terminal. The only way out, and it closes without notice.

SC-HOSPITAL-GATE.note: The hospital you can see and the permit you need to reach it.

SC-ROOFTOP-TANKS.note: Black water tanks and solar heaters on a flat roof. Where you go when the power is on six hours a day.

SC-RUBBLE.note: A house that had a building permit refused, and then had no house.

SC-BOMBED-ROOM.note: Where the Palestinian run opens and, thirty seconds later, ends. A domestic room with the ceiling gone and an unexploded bomb standing in the middle of it, absurdly large. The absurdity is the point: it is too big to be a surprise and nobody in the room is reacting to it.

SC-CLASSROOM-PS.note: PS variant of SC-CLASSROOM. A unrwa school classroom in the west bank, breeze-block walls, double desks, a blackboard, one window with the glass taped.

SC-HOME-DAY-PS.note: PS variant of SC-HOME-DAY. The front room of a palestinian family house in daylight, tiled floor, low couches against three walls, a framed photograph.

SC-STREET-DAY-PS.note: PS variant of SC-STREET-DAY. A street in nablus in daylight, stone buildings, shuttered shops, steep steps, water tanks on every roof.

SC-REGISTRY-PS.note: PS variant of SC-REGISTRY. A palestinian authority civil registry counter, arabic forms in trays, a ledger, a queue rail.

SC-DESK-NIGHT-PS.note: PS variant of SC-DESK-NIGHT. A cluttered desk at night in a west bank flat, laptop glow, papers, a glass of tea.

SC-COURTYARD-PS.note: PS variant of SC-COURTYARD. A walled courtyard of a palestinian village house, a fig tree, olive oil tins stacked by the door, stone paving.
