start.text: You were born.
Nablus. A room above your grandmother's, with one window and a gas heater that is turned off when guests leave.
He's here. Bassam - he's here.
Your mother is Rana. She teaches Arabic at a school fifteen minutes away, or ninety, depending on the road.
There is an unexploded bomb standing upright in the middle of the room. It is taller than your father. It has been there for the entire scene.
Nobody has mentioned it. It is not remarkable enough to mention.

options.text: I open my eyes.
options.note: there is nothing else you can do

options.text: I cry until somebody comes.
options.note: it works; it will keep working for about four seconds

options.text: I look at the bomb.

eyes.text: Lamp. Ceiling, or where the ceiling was. A face. The face is enormous and it is crying.

cry.text: Somebody comes immediately. This is the last time in your life that asking will work this well.

bomb.text: It is grey, and finned, and it has stencilled lettering on the side in a language nobody in this room reads.

died.text: You were four days old. You did not do anything. There is no decision you could have made differently, and the game is not going to pretend otherwise by offering you one.

options.text: Do I want to be reincarnated? Yes.
options.note: there is another life waiting, and it is this one again

options.text: No.

yes.text: Good. There is another one ready.

no.text: You do not have that choice.
You must be born again, here, and suffer again. That is the whole of the arrangement and nobody is going to ask your opinion of it a second time.

again.text: You are born again, in the same room, to the same mother, with the same bomb in it.
This time it does not go off. That is the only difference between a life and the one you just had.
You survive the first year. It is the only achievement that will never once be asked for on a form.

the-hawiyya-and-the-registry.title: The number that is not issued by your own government

start.text: Your father registers your birth. The counter is Palestinian: the clerk is from Nablus, the forms are in Arabic.
What she types goes into the Israeli population registry. The Palestinian Authority may enter names into it. It may not add a person to it, or remove one, without Israeli approval.
Full name, please. Spell it for me.

options.text: I am not here - my father says it for me.
(Years later he will tell you he said it clearly.)

father.text: She types. The keyboard is Arabic; the registry field underneath is Hebrew, transliterated by whoever is at the counter.

options.text: I cannot object. I am four days old.
My father does not notice for six years.

issued.text: You are issued a hawiyya number: nine digits, beginning with a digit that says which authority holds your file.
The hawiyya is the green identity card carried by Palestinians of the West Bank. Green is not blue. Blue is Jerusalem, and blue can be taken away.
{document}. Keep the paper. You will need it for everything, all your life.

options.text: I ask, later, why the spelling is wrong.
Nobody asks. It is the spelling now.

why.text: It's what was entered. To change it you apply to the registry, and the registry is not ours.

final.text: From now on every permit, every crossing and every officer will read {document}. Your mother will go on calling you {player}.
Remember this: {document} is the ENGLISH name you have forever. It is the one on the hawiyya, on the tasreeh, and on every document that decides where you may stand.

start.text: Your grandmother Nawal bakes on a taboun - a domed clay oven lined with hot stones. The bread comes out dimpled where the stones touched it.
Come here, {player}. Hands.

options.text: I hold my hands out.
I ask if I can put the za'atar on myself.

hands.text: She tears the bread, pours olive oil until it runs, and presses za'atar into it with her thumb.

self.text: Too much. Always too much. Go on.
You use far too much za'atar. It is the best thing you have eaten in your life.

eat.text: The oil is from your family's trees, pressed in October, stored in a tin behind the door.
Nothing about this requires permission from anyone. Remember that it did not.

the-teacher-who-decided.title: The teacher who decided you were clever

start.text: Forty children. One teacher, Miss Abeer, who has marked exercise books by torchlight twice this month because the power was out.
Who can tell me what this word means?

options.text: I put my hand up.
options.note: you are not certain you are right

options.text: I say nothing and hope she asks me.

hand.text: You are right. She does not make a fuss of it, which is why you remember it.

wait.text: She asks you. She had already decided to.

after.text: She gives you a book that is too old for you and tells you to bring it back when you have finished it, not before.

options.text: I ask if I can keep it.
I promise to bring it back.

keep.text: You'll do something. Make sure it's something you chose.
Nine seconds of an adult's attention. It will hold for twenty years.

start.text: The road to your grandmother's village is eleven kilometres. It takes twenty minutes, or two hours, and you cannot know which before you set out.
Between you and the rest of the West Bank there are, by the UN's count, more than nine hundred physical obstacles: checkpoints, road gates, earth mounds, trenches, concrete blocks.
Sit still, {player}. Don't stare at them. Don't hide either.

options.text: I sit on my hands.
I ask why we are stopping.

ask.text: Because they decided to stop us. That's the whole reason.

wait.text: The queue does not move for forty minutes. Nobody explains. There is nobody whose job it is to explain.

options.text: I watch my father hand over the card.
I look at the floor of the car.

card.text: Your father hands the green card through the window. The soldier is perhaps nineteen. He looks at the card for a long time, in the way people do when they are bored rather than suspicious.

options.text: I ask if we can go to the village now.
I say nothing until we have driven away.

closed.text: You are waved through. Today the obstacle cost you ninety minutes and nothing else.
You are eight. You have just learned that the length of a journey is a decision somebody else makes on the day.

start.text: A flat piece of ground between two buildings. Two stones for one goal, a paint mark for the other.
{player}, you're in goal. You're always in goal.

options.text: I go in goal.
I refuse and demand to play up front.

goal.text: You let in four. Nobody cares. Samir takes his shirt off and swings it over his head for a goal that was clearly offside.

front.text: You play up front, score once, and talk about it for the rest of the year.

dusk.text: I'm going to be a physiotherapist. For a club. A real one.

options.text: I tell him he'd be good at it.
I ask how you even become that here.

how.text: You study. Then you go somewhere. That's all it is.
Neither of you says the second part out loud, which is that going somewhere is the difficult half.

end_scene.text: It gets dark. Nobody wants to be the one who says it is over.

start.text: October. The whole family goes up to the terraces: your parents, Nawal, two uncles, cousins who have been told they are helping.
Nets go down under the trees. You strip the branches by hand and the olives rain onto the net with a sound like applause.
Not like that, {player}. You'll break next year's wood.

options.text: I let her show me how.
I climb higher instead.

show.text: She takes your hand and moves it down the branch, thumb leading. Her mother taught her on the same terrace.

climb.text: From the top of the tree you can see the village, the road, and the red roofs of the settlement on the next hill.

lunch.text: Lunch is bread, oil from last year, tomatoes, and tea made on a gas ring balanced on a stone.
This tree was my grandfather's. That one nobody remembers planting.

options.text: I ask how old they are.
I eat and say nothing.

old.text: Older than the country. Any of them.

done.text: The oil will be pressed within two days and will last the year. Nothing today required a permit.

start.text: The upper terraces are now behind the fence of the settlement's security perimeter. The trees are still yours. The access is not.
To reach them your father applies for harvest coordination: a written arrangement, made through the District Coordination Office, that lets a named family onto its own land on named days.
They gave us one day. For sixty trees.

options.text: I ask what happens if we need two.
I ask who decides how many days.

two.text: Then the rest stays on the tree.

who.text: The army. With the settlement's view taken into account.

day.text: On the day, the gate opens at nine and will close at three. Six hours, eight people, sixty trees.
Two settlers watch from the ridge. A soldier stands between, which is either protection or supervision depending on the hour.

options.text: I pick as fast as I can.
I stop and look up at the ridge.

fast.text: You get through forty trees. Your hands are raw. Twenty trees keep their fruit until it drops.

look.text: You pick. He is not frightened of them exactly; he is frightened of what a photograph of you looking would be used for.

close.text: It is ten past two. Nobody argues about the twenty minutes, because arguing is how a coordination is refused next year.

options.text: I carry the crates down.
I ask the soldier for the extra twenty minutes.

askmore.text: He is not angry. He simply has no mechanism for saying yes.

done.text: The oil this year is two thirds of last year's. The trees are fine. It is the access that is smaller.

start.text: You are nineteen and you are applying for your first passport: the Palestinian Authority travel document, dark green, issued in Ramallah.
It costs 250 shekels and takes three weeks. Your mother comes with you and pretends it is because she is going that way anyway.
Photograph. Hawiyya. Both parents' names.

options.text: I hand everything over.
I check the spelling on the form first.

check.text: The form already says {document}. It was copied from the registry, which was copied from a clerk's ear, nineteen years ago.

hand.text: Three weeks later it arrives. It is the first document you have ever owned that is meant to take you out of here.

options.text: I open it and read every page.
I put it somewhere safe immediately.

read.text: Photograph, dates, a number. On the page where other passports print a nationality, this one prints something else - but you do not know that yet, because you have never seen another passport.

safe.text: It goes in the tin behind the door, with the deeds and the olive oil receipts.

out.text: Today it is a passport and you are a person who could go somewhere. That feeling is real. Keep it.

a-travel-document-not-a-nationality.title: The field that does not say a nationality

start.text: You are filling in an online application for a conference in Amman. It wants your passport details.
The form has a dropdown headed NATIONALITY. You scroll it twice.

options.text: I look for Palestine in the list.
I look at what my passport actually says.

list.text: Some forms have it. Some have "Palestinian Territories". Some have nothing, and then you have to choose between a country you are not from and leaving it blank.

field.text: Your passport is a travel document. It certifies that a named authority will accept you back. It is not proof of citizenship of a state, because the state whose citizenship it would be is not one the issuing authority fully controls.
It gets you across borders. It doesn't get you the thing other people's passports get them.

options.text: I ask what that thing is.
I ask if it will be a problem for the visa.

thing.text: A government that has to take your side. You have a document. You don't have that.

visa.text: It will be a question. Every time. Answer it the same way every time.

out.text: You select the option nearest to true and submit the form.

the-scholarship-you-cannot-take.title: Winning it, and not being able to go

start.text: An email at eleven at night. You read it four times before you believe the first line.
Dear {document}, we are delighted to offer you a fully funded place on the MSc in Civil Engineering, with a stipend, commencing in September.

options.text: I shout for my mother.
I sit still and read it again.

shout.text: What? What is it? {player}, read it to me properly.
You read it out loud. Your father makes tea at midnight, which he does for exactly two occasions.

still.text: Fully funded. A stipend. Nothing in the email is conditional on anything except you saying yes.

problem.text: To take it up you must leave. To leave you must cross at Allenby - the King Hussein Bridge into Jordan - because you may not use Ben Gurion airport, and reach the British consulate for the visa.
The crossing requires that your name is not flagged on the day. There is no way to check in advance, and no appeal that runs faster than the start of term.
Apply for the visa first. If the bridge is going to be a problem, be a person with a visa when it happens.

options.text: I book the earliest date I can.
I ask what the odds actually are.

odds.text: Most people get through. That is not the same as you getting through. Book it early so there's room to fail once.

book.text: You accept the offer. September is eleven weeks away, and every one of them now depends on a decision nobody will make until you are standing in front of them.

the-magnetic-card-and-the-permit.title: A work permit tied to one employer

start.text: September did not happen. The bridge is a story for later. You need to earn, and the work that pays is on the other side of the Green Line.
To work there you need two things. A magnetic card - a security clearance issued after a check you cannot see. And a tasreeh: the work permit itself.
The permit is issued to the employer. Not to you.

options.text: I ask what that means in practice.
I ask how long it lasts.

means.text: You may work for him. Not for anyone else. If he stops employing you, the permit stops.

long.text: Two months. Then it is applied for again. By him.

catch.text: So the document that lets you work is owned by the person paying you, is renewed by him, and ends when he says so.
It also prints the hours. Yours says you may be on that side between 05:00 and 19:00. Being there at 19:10 is not lateness. It is being unlawfully present.

options.text: I take the permit.
I ask what happens if the checkpoint queue makes me late.

late.text: That is not a reason on the form. There is no box for the queue.

take.text: You take it. It is the best thing available and it is worse than any job you have ever heard described on television.

the-broker-who-sells-your-own-permit.title: Paying for a permit that is supposed to be free

start.text: The employer's permit did not come through. A man called Khalil can get you one. Everybody knows a Khalil.
Twenty-two hundred shekels a month. You start Sunday.

options.text: I ask what the money is for.
I ask why the permit costs anything at all.

forwhat.text: For the permit. For the arrangement. For me.

free.text: It is free. To the employer. He applies, he pays nothing. Then he sells the slot.

truth.text: A permit issued at no cost to a registered employer is worth money to a worker who has no other way to reach the work. So the slot is sold, sometimes by the employer, sometimes by a broker, usually by both in sequence.
Two thousand two hundred shekels is roughly a third of what you will earn. You will pay it monthly, in cash, for as long as you want the job.

options.text: I pay it.
options.note: it is the only route to the work

options.text: I ask whether I can report this.
I walk away.

report.text: To who? The permit is legal. The job is legal. The money is a favour between friends.
He is not wrong in any way that a complaint form could capture. The transaction leaves no document with his name on it.

walk.text: You walk away. Two weeks later you come back, because the alternative work pays a third as much and your mother has stopped asking how the job search is going.

pay.text: You pay. Your wage is now a number minus a number, and only one of them appears on any piece of paper.

a-wedding-in-the-village.title: A wedding in the village your family is from

start.text: Your cousin's wedding, in the village, in the courtyard, with four hundred people who are all in some way related to you.
There is a dabke line that has been going for an hour. Somebody's uncle has a microphone and will not be parted from it.
{player}, I don't know the steps.

options.text: I pull her into the line anyway.
I show her the steps at the edge first.

line.text: She is terrible at it for ninety seconds and then she is not. Your grandmother watches this and decides something.

teach.text: Six steps, repeated. You count them out loud like an idiot and she learns them in a minute.

nawal.text: That one. Bring that one to me properly.

options.text: I tell her we're getting married.
I say we're just friends, badly.

badly.text: Yes. I am ninety and I am blind. Bring her.

tell.text: Huda is registered in Gaza. She came to the West Bank six years ago on a permit to study and has not been able to leave or regularise since.
Tonight this is a detail about where somebody is from. It will not stay a detail.

living-together-illegally-at-home.title: Married, and one of you is not allowed to be here

start.text: You are married. You live in Ramallah. Your wife's hawiyya says her registered address is in Gaza.

To change that address - to be recorded as living where she actually lives - requires Israeli approval of a change to the population registry. Since 2000 those approvals have been frozen almost entirely.
So I am here, and on paper I am not here.

options.text: I ask what happens if she's stopped.
I ask how we fix it.

fix.text: You apply. It goes into a queue that has not moved for most applicants in twenty years. You keep applying so that there is a record of you trying.

stopped.text: If she is stopped at a checkpoint with a Gaza-registered address, she can be removed to Gaza. Not charged. Returned.
Not to prison. To the place her file says she belongs, through a crossing that may not let her come back.

options.text: I ask how likely that is.
I ask her what she wants to do.

likely.text: Unlikely on a Tuesday. Likely enough that she should think about which roads she takes.

her.text: I want to go to my sister's. She's forty minutes away and I haven't been in four years.

options.text: I say we'll go.
I say not this month.

go.text: You take the long road, the one with fewer checkpoints and an extra hour. You do this for the next eleven years.

no.text: She does not argue. That is worse than if she had.

out.text: Your marriage is lawful. Your household is not a category the registry recognises.

the-permit-for-the-hospital.title: The medical permit, and the difference between no and nothing

start.text: Your mother's biopsy comes back. The treatment she needs is at Augusta Victoria, in East Jerusalem - thirty-one kilometres from her front door.
She has a green West Bank hawiyya. To enter Jerusalem she needs a medical permit, applied for through Palestinian liaison, approved on the Israeli side, valid for the date of the appointment.
Apply now. Today. The appointment is in eleven days and the permit is not quick.

options.text: I ask what happens if it doesn't come.
I fill in the application there and then.

ifnot.text: Then she misses the cycle, and we start the conversation again in three weeks.

apply.text: The application goes in with her hawiyya number, the referral, and the appointment letter. You are told to phone the liaison office to check.
You phone every day. On the ninth day you get an answer.
There is no response on the file.

options.text: I ask whether that means refused.
I ask who I can speak to.

refused.text: No. Refused is an answer. There is no answer.
A refusal can be appealed, because a refusal is a decision. Silence is not a decision, so there is nothing to appeal and nobody who is required to produce one.

speak.text: I phone the same number you would phone. Today it rang out.

day.text: On the morning of the appointment there is still no answer. You drive her to the checkpoint anyway, because the permit sometimes appears in the system on the day.

options.text: I take her to the checkpoint.
I phone the hospital and rebook.

gate.text: Not in the system. Go back.
He is not being cruel. He is reading a screen that has nothing on it, which is exactly what silence looks like from his side.

rebook.text: The next slot is in twenty-six days. You take it, and start the permit application again from the beginning.

out.text: She starts treatment five weeks after the date on the referral. Nobody ever refused anything.

the-building-permit-that-is-not-issued.title: Building without the permit that is not granted

start.text: Your uncle's land is in Area C: the 60% of the West Bank under full Israeli civil and military control, where Palestinian building requires an Israeli permit.
He applied for one. So did most of his village. In recent years the great majority of such applications have been refused.
He waited nine years. Then his son got married.

options.text: I ask what he did.
I ask why he didn't just wait.

wait.text: Wait for what? The answer was not going to change. He needed a room.

did.text: He built two rooms and a roof, without the permit, on his own registered land, which is what almost everyone in that situation does.
Eleven months later the demolition order arrived. Then, one Tuesday at six in the morning, the machines.

options.text: I go and stand with him.
I ask whether he can appeal.

appeal.text: He can. It costs more than the building did and it almost never succeeds. The demolition happens anyway while it runs.

stand.text: It takes forty minutes. Afterwards he is charged the cost of the machines that did it.
That's the part people don't believe. He pays for it.

options.text: I help him carry out what's left.
I ask if he'll build again.

again.text: He says yes, in the tone of a man stating a fact about the weather. He rebuilds within the year.

out.text: The land is still his. That was never the question.

electricity-by-the-hour.title: Six hours on, twelve hours off

start.text: Huda's family in Gaza have power for a fixed number of hours a day, on a published rota that everyone plans their life around.
You are on the phone to her mother, who is talking fast because the schedule says the power goes in nine minutes.

options.text: I ask how they manage the fridge.
I ask what happens to the water.

fridge.text: You do not fill a fridge. You buy what is eaten that day. The cost of food goes up because you cannot buy in quantity.

water.text: The water is pumped to the roof tanks electrically. No power means no pumping, so a long outage is also no water on the upper floors.
That's why the tanks. You fill everything when it's on.

options.text: I ask about the hospital she works near.
I ask whether a generator fixes it.

generator.text: A generator needs fuel, which is imported under restriction, expensive, and rationed when supply is cut. The generator is a way of being slightly less affected, not a solution.

hospital.text: Hospitals run on generators and prioritise: theatres and neonatal first, then dialysis, then everything else. Lifts are everything else.

cut.text: The line goes quiet mid-sentence. Not dropped - the power went, and with it the router.

options.text: I call back in the morning.
I sit on the roof for a while.

roof.text: From your roof you can see other roofs, all of them crowded with black tanks, all of them the same answer to the same problem.

out.text: You call back in the morning. She answers as if nothing had happened, because for her nothing had.

allenby-the-only-gateway.title: The bridge, and what happens when it shuts

start.text: There is no Palestinian airport. Ben Gurion is forty minutes away and closed to you. The way out of the West Bank is the King Hussein Bridge into Jordan, and then a flight from Amman.
You leave at three in the morning for a crossing that opens at eight, because the queue forms in the dark.
Take food. Take the charger. Take everything.

options.text: I join the queue.
I ask how long it usually takes.

howlong.text: Four hours. Or fourteen. Or they close it and you come home and try on Sunday.

queue.text: Buses, then a terminal hall, then a numbered booth. Your passport goes through a window and does not come back.

options.text: I ask how long I'll be waiting.
I sit down.

sit.text: Three hours. Nobody tells you anything, and there is nobody to ask, because the person who took the passport has gone off shift.
You are not being punished. You are simply inside a process with no published timings and no obligation to explain itself.

options.text: I wait.
I go and knock on the window.

knock.text: Every person in the hall watches you sit back down. Several of them have been here longer than you.

wait.text: At five past four your name is called - the registry spelling, pronounced badly - and the passport comes back with a stamp.

options.text: I ask what the three hours were for.
I take it and go.

why.text: He has already turned to the next person. The question does not have an addressee.

out.text: You are in Jordan. It took thirteen hours to travel the distance you could see from the hill above your grandmother's house.

held-at-the-border-with-a-valid-visa.title: A valid visa is permission to travel, not permission to enter

start.text: Toronto Pearson. You are flying on to a conference in Chicago, and US border control happens here, before you board - it is called preclearance.
You have a valid US visa in your travel document. It took four months, two interviews and a fee you did not get back when the first application was returned.
{document}? Step out of the line, sir.

options.text: I ask what the problem is.
I step out of the line.

problem.text: It has been random on every flight you have ever taken.

step.text: A side room with eleven chairs. Your passport and phone go into a tray. Nobody says how long.
Here is the thing nobody explains before you travel: a visa is permission to ask to enter. The decision is made at the border, by the officer in front of you, and it is not appealable there.

options.text: I ask whether I can call someone.
I wait quietly.
I ask to see a supervisor.

quiet.text: Ninety minutes. A family opposite has been there longer and has stopped talking to each other.

super.text: I am the supervisor for this room.

options.text: I say the name of the town.
I say what my documents say.

town.text: There is a correct answer to this question and you do not know which one it is today.

docs.text: I didn't ask what the document says. I asked where you were born.

end_beat.text: After two hours and ten minutes they return your passport and wave you through without a word about why.
You make the flight by eleven minutes. The conference is fine. You spend the first hour of it steadying your hands.
